thread.title: Oil turns higher as supply relief offsets stock-market drop

author: Rachel Koning Beals
title: Oil turns higher as supply relief offsets stock-market drop
text:
Oil prices moved lower in volatile trading Thursday, tracking the drop in the stock market which contributed to concerns over the economy and a potential decline in energy demand.
A volatile crude market on Wednesday sent prices to two-week highs by settlement time , after a reported drop in December crude exports emerged from Saudi Arabia . At a meeting in December, OPEC and nonmember producers that include Russia agreed to cut production by 1.2 million barrels from October 2018 levels, effective January, for an initial period of six months. They plan to review output levels in April.
“Bottom line, the drop in Saudi exports was a welcome surprise for the bulls [Wednesday], but the longer-term outlook and broader fundamental backdrop are still not overly encouraging,” analysts said in the latest Sevens Report.
“And while there are signs that a near-term bottom may be forming in the low $40s for WTI, there is significant resistance on the charts in the low $50s,” they said. “It will likely take a more material bullish development for prices to begin a longer-term uptrend as oversupply fears are still the primary influence.”
Against that backdrop, West Texas Intermediate crude for February delivery CLG9, +0.49% shed 47 cents, or 1%, to trade at $46.07 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Front-month WTI crude futures dropped by 24.8% in 2018, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
The global benchmark, March Brent crude UK:LCOG9 meanwhile, lost 40 cents, or 0.7%, to $54.51 a barrel on ICE Futures Europe. The international benchmark finished last year with a loss of 19.5%.

Oil’s upside has been limited in part by concerns about the global economy, especially after the latest round of worrying statistics out of China, and its potential impact on demand for crude. Demand is also in question as wealth is wiped out of stock markets, the latest blow due to a sales warning from Apple AAPL, -8.36%
AAPL, -8.36% Still, major crude producers, including the U.S. and Russia, continued to ramp up output in the second half of 2018. The U.S. Energy Information Administration forecasts American output will rise to 12.1 million barrels a day in 2019, up 1.2 million barrels a day from the previous year.
“News of record production by Russia and the U.S., along with Iraqi exports surging, weighed on prices” early Thursday, said consulting firm Global Risk Management in a note.
Rounding out the action in the energy market, February gasoline RBG9, +1.38% traded at $1.323 a gallon, down 0.2% on Nymex, while February heating oil HOG9, +1.38% added 0.4% to $1.708 a gallon.
February natural gas NGG19, -1.08% fell 2.2% to $2.894 per million British thermal units. It trades more than 10% lower week to date.
On Friday morning, the Energy Information Administration will release its weekly data on U.S. natural-gas supplies, followed by the weekly report on domestic petroleum stockpiles. Both are delayed this week because of Tuesday’s New Year’s Day holiday.
The American Petroleum Institute, a trade group, will release its weekly domestic petroleum inventory report later Thursday, which has also been delayed due to the holiday.
“Current market estimates expect a drop in U.S. crude stocks,” which could help crude prices distance themselves from recent lows, said Robbie Fraser, global commodity analyst at Schneider Electric.
